abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR T-cell) therapy has become an established treatment option for relapsed or refractory large B-cell lymphoma, offering durable remission in some previously incurable cases. However, the effective management of immune-mediated toxicities, particularly cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS), remains critical to ensure safety. Treatment algorithms have been proposed based on the American Society for Transplantation and Cellular Therapy consensus grading system by the Joint Accreditation Committee of the International Society for Cellular Therapy and the European Group for Blood and Marrow Transplantation, as well as the National Comprehensive Cancer Network guidelines. Recently, early intervention to ensure that CAR T-cell therapy is performed safely has also been proposed. This review provides an update and overview of the treatment strategies for CRS and ICANS in CAR T-cell therapy for malignant lymphoma.

sec.p: Keywords: chimeric antigen receptor T-cell, CAR-T, cytokine release syndrome, immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome, cytokine
Received 2025 Nov 7; Revised 2025 Nov 20; Accepted 2025 Nov 20; Collection date 2025 Dec.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Recently, chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR T-cell) therapy has been widely used for relapsed and refractory malignant lymphoma, which can provide long-term disease control in some cases that were previously difficult to cure.1 Meanwhile, it is essential to manage adverse events properly in CAR T-cell therapy. Once CAR T-cells bind to target antigens expressed on tumor cells, they become activated and release granzyme and perforin, resulting in anti-tumor effects (Figure 1). Simultaneously, CAR T-cells activate the surrounding immune cells (such as macrophages) by releasing various cytokines such as TNFα, GM-CSF, and IFNγ.2 Furthermore, damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) which are released from lymphoma cells in response to CAR T-cell attacks activate immune cells and promote the release of additional cytokines.3

caption.p: Anti-tumor effects and adverse events associated with CAR T-cell therapy.

Once CAR T-cells bind to target antigens expressed on tumor cells, they become activated and release granzyme and perforin (Anti-tumor effect). Simultaneously, CAR T-cells activate surrounding immune cells by releasing various cytokines. Furthermore, damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) released from lymphoma cells in response to CAR T cell attack activate immune cells and promote additional cytokine release. As a result, massive cytokine release may cause CRS and ICANS (Adverse events).

sec.p: Cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS) are a series of adverse events caused by elevated concentrations of various cytokines in the blood.2 CRS is a common complication of CAR T-cell therapy, characterized by the excessive release of inflammatory cytokines. It typically occurs within days to a week after administration and presents with fever, worsening respiratory status, and decreased blood pressure.4 ICANS often occurs slightly later than CRS, presenting with symptoms such as depressed level of consciousness, seizures, motor weakness, and cerebral edema.4 In most cases, CRS and ICANS are transient and improve with appropriate management; however, severe cases may require intensive care unit (ICU) management. It has been reported that the blood levels of representative cytokines released into the bloodstream, such as IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, IL-15, IFN-γ, MCP-1, MIP-1α, MIP-1β, and GM-CSF, correlate with the severity of CRS and ICANS.3 Excessive cytokine release, particularly IL-6, is known to be involved not only in CRS and ICANS, but also in the subsequent development of prolonged cytopenia.5
Since control of CRS and ICANS is crucial in CAR T-cell therapy, in this review, we summarize CRS and ICANS, including management strategies.

sec.title: DATA FROM CLINICAL TRIALS AND REAL-WORLD EVIDENCE
Clinical trial6–11
sec.p: CRS and ICANS outcomes in representative clinical trials for large B-cell lymphoma (LBCL) are shown in Table 1. The incidence of CRS and ICANS in clinical trials varies depending on the type of CAR T-cells and the evaluation method used. Many prior clinical trials have used the Lee criteria to evaluate CRS and ICANS.12 Generally, it is known that CAR T-cells with CD28 as the co-stimulatory molecule are associated with a higher incidence and severity of CRS and ICANS in comparison to those with 4-1BB. In clinical trials of axicabtagene ciloleucel (axi-cel), which contains CD28 as a co-stimulatory molecule, the incidence of CRS and ICANS tended to be high. In the JULIET trial, despite using tisagenlecleucel (tisa-cel), which contains 4-1BB as a co-stimulatory molecule on CAR T-cells, the incidence of severe CRS tended to be higher.13 It is possible that interventions for CRS were less frequent or delayed in the JULIET trial, which was conducted in the early era of the clinical development of CAR T-cell therapy. Recently, treatment interventions are being initiated earlier, which may explain the lower incidence of CRS observed in trials other than the JULIET trial.

sec.title: Real-world data13–21
sec.p: Recently, real-world data on tisa-cel, axi-cel, and lisocabtagene maraleucel (liso-cel) have been reported (Table 2, 3 and Supplementary Table 1). Although many real-world studies used American Society for Transplantation and Cellular Therapy (ASTCT) consensus grading system that were different from those in prior clinical trials, incidence rate of CRS and ICANS were consistent with those observed in prior clinical trials.4 CRS typically appears within a few days after CAR T-cell infusion (at the latest within two weeks) and generally resolves within a few days to two weeks with appropriate management. With appropriate management using tocilizumab and steroids, the incidence of severe CRS (grade ≥3) is controlled to less than 10% in most of real-world reports. Most ICANS cases tend to develop several days after the onset of CRS. The incidence of severe ICANS (grade ≥3) was 1.1–7.4% for tisa-cel, 10–19% for liso-cel, and 16.6–34% for axi-cel, tending to be higher with axi-cel. However, these results were based on retrospective analyses, and it is important to note that the timing of intervention and patient background may differ across reports.

sec.title: RISK FACTORS FOR CRS AND ICANS
sec.p: Research is progressing on markers that can predict the severity of CRS and ICANS. According to data from the DESCART registry in France, factors significantly associated with the incidence of severe CRS (grade ≥3) included high tumor burden, poor disease control prior to lymphodepletion therapy, platelet count <150,000/μL, and elevated LDH and CRP levels.21 On the other hand, factors significantly associated with the incidence of severe ICANS (grade ≥3) included female sex, platelet count <150,000/μL, poor disease control prior to lymphocyte depletion therapy, and the use of axi-cel. A Nagoya University group reported that a fever of ≥38.6 degrees celsius within 24 hours after axi-cel administration is an indicator predicting serious CRS and ICANS.22

There have been reports on the association between biomarkers and severity of CRS and ICANS. CRP is known to increase depending on IL-6 concentration. The Moffitt Cancer Center reported that baseline serum IL-6 concentrations ≥40 pg/mL prior to axi-cel cell infusion were associated with a shorter time to CRS onset and higher incidence of severe CRS.23 They also examined the relationship between the tumor microenvironment and toxicity. Lower T-cell infiltration within tumor cells, higher macrophage activation, and the lower expression of Foxp3 (a regulatory T-cell marker) have been reported to be associated with a higher likelihood of severe neurotoxicity.

The US Lymphoma CAR T Consortium investigated the relationship between severe CRS and ICANS following axi-cel cell infusion. A multivariate analysis showed that poor performance status and elevated serum bilirubin levels were correlated with severe CRS, and high tumor burden was correlated with severe ICANS.16

Data from over 1,100 patients receiving tisa-cel in the CIBMTR registry showed significantly higher CRS and/or ICANS rates in patients with ECOG PS ≥2 and elevated LDH.13 This registry also showed a lower incidence of grade ≥3 CRS in comparison to the JULIET trial. It is thought that tocilizumab was used in many grade ≥3 cases in the JULIET trial, whereas tocilizumab is initiated in grade 1–2 cases in the real-world settings.

A sub analysis of the ZUMA-7 trial showed that higher numbers of infused effector T cells in axi-cel product was associated with an increased risk of grade ≥3 neurotoxicity after infusion.24 On the other hand, this analysis found no association between the number of infused effector T cells in axi-cel product and the incidence of grade ≥3 CRS.

Differences in the genetic background may also be involved in the onset of CRS and ICANS. Interestingly, in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL), the incidence of CRS tended to be higher in the Japanese real-world data from the SETUP trial than in the US CIBMTR real-world data.13,15 The reason for this is unknown, but it may be influenced by differences in patient background, disease status, treatment interventions for CRS, and potential racial or genetic background differences.

sec.title: GENERAL APPROACH TO THE PATIENTS WITH CRS AND ICANS
sec.p: While various evaluation methods exist for CRS and ICANS, the ASTCT consensus grading system is widely used.4

sec.title: Management of CRS
sec.p: Based on this ASTCT consensus grading, the Joint Accreditation Committee of the International Society for Cellular Therapy and the European and European Group for Blood and Marrow Transplantation (JACIE) has proposed a treatment algorithm.25 The following are the main recommendations for the use of tocilizumab and dexamethasone from the JACIE’s algorithm. IL-6 is known to be key mediators of CRS. Tocilizumab, an anti-IL-6 receptor antibody, is clinically used as a first-line treatment option. For grade 1 CRS, consider administration of tocilizumab. For grade 2 CRS, tocilizumab administration is recommended. For grade 2 CRS with a poor response to tocilizumab, or for grade 3 CRS, administer 10 mg of dexamethasone every 6 hours for 1–3 days. If the effect of 10 mg of dexamethasone was insufficient, the dose is increased to 20 mg. For grade 4 CRS, administer 20 mg of dexamethasone; if the response is insufficient, the patient is switched to steroid pulse therapy. Notably, when fever occurs after CAR T-cell infusion, it is difficult to judge whether the fever is due to CRS or other causes (e.g., infection). Therefore, when fever occurs, it is recommended to check for the presence of an infectious event through various culture tests and imaging examinations such as computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).

The National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines also provide treatment algorithms for CRS and ICANS, based on the ASTCT consensus grading system.26 The treatment algorithms and approaches were generally consistent with those of the JACIE. However, slightly different approaches have been used for treatment interventions. The administration of tocilizumab should be considered for grade 1 CRS. Even in grade 1 CRS, if fever occurs within 72 hours of CAR T-cell infusion, the administration of dexamethasone (10 mg, daily) is recommended. For grade 2 CRS, dexamethasone (10 mg, every 12–24 hours) and tocilizumab are administered. If improvement is not observed within 24 hours after initiating tocilizumab for grade 2 CRS, management should follow that for ICANS grade 3. For grade 3 CRS, dexamethasone (10 mg, every 6–12 hours) and tocilizumab are administered. If it is treatment resistant, treatment should be administered according to grade 4 ICANS. Regarding the use of tocilizumab, if symptoms do not improve, repeat administration should be performed more with a >8 hours interval, but a maximum of four doses is recommended. For grade 4 CRS, administer dexamethasone 10 mg every 6 hours; if treatment resistance is observed, it is switched to steroid pulse therapy. If resistant to these treatments, other therapies, such as IL-1 receptor antagonist (anakinra), antithymocyte globulin (ATG), cyclophosphamide, JAK inhibitor (ruxolitinib), or IL-6 antagonists (siltuximab) may be considered.27

sec.title: Management of ICANS
sec.p: In the JACIE algorithm, for grade 1 ICANS, close monitoring of electroencephalograph (EEG), a cerebrospinal fluid analysis, and brain MRI are recommended. For grade ≥2 ICANS, the administration of dexamethasone (10 mg every 6 hours) for 1 to 3 days is recommended. If seizures occur, levetiracetam or benzodiazepine should be considered to administer. The patient should be switched to steroid pulse therapy if improvement is not achieved with dexamethasone. If it is resistant to these treatments, other treatments such as anakinra or siltuximab are considered.27

The NCCN guidelines recommend more intensive treatment interventions in comparison to the JACIE algorithm.26 In the NCCN guidelines, for grade 1 or 2 ICANS, single 10 mg dose of dexamethasone administration is recommended and re-assess after each dose. If improvement is not achieved with a single 10 mg dose of dexamethasone, repeat dosing every 6–12 hours and re-assessment is recommended. For grade 3 ICANS, dexamethasone (10 mg) every 6 hours or methylprednisolone (1 mg/kg) every 12 hours is recommended. For grade 4 ICANS, management in an intensive care unit is considered. In addition, steroid pulse therapy should be administered and adding anakinra should be considered if it is ineffective. For grade ≥3 ICANS, imaging evaluations with CT or MRI every 2 to 3 days should be consider. If concurrent CRS is present, tocilizumab administration in combination with steroids should be considered.

sec.title: Utilization of the ICE score in ICANS assessment
sec.p: Assessment using the immune effector cell-associated encephalopathy (ICE) score is very important when evaluating ICANS (Table 4). The ICE score is used to evaluate ICANS in the ASTCT consensus grading system.4 Among the questions in the ICE score, writing disability is a useful finding for detecting early symptoms of ICANS (Figure 2) In addition, after CAR T-cell infusion, it is important to maintain contact with family and/or friends via short messages on social media. In the early stages of ICANS, similar to writing disabilities, patients often experience an inability to send messages.

caption.p: The patient with DLBCL presented with grade 1 CRS from day 1. For Grade 1 CRS, patient received tocilizumab on day 1 and dexamethasone 10 mg iv once or twice daily for 5 days from day1. On day 6, writing disability was observed and ICE assessment showed a score of 1. Therefore, the patient was treated with steroid pulse therapy for three days. Within several hours of starting steroid pulse therapy, an improvement in writing disability was observed.

sec.title: CONCLUSION
sec.p: As CAR T-cell therapy has become widely used as a standard treatment, it is essential to perform it safely. In recent years, there has been a trend toward earlier treatment intervention for CRS and ICANS. In particular, aggressive treatment is required when CRS develops early after CAR T-cell infusion. For ICANS, early detection is crucial. A team-based approach involving family and friends is required for CAR T-cell therapy.
